newsitem.title: JAPAN: Car sales in Japan slip again in July.
newsitem.headline: Car sales in Japan slip again in July.

text.p: The skid in car sales in Japan stretched into a fourth successive month in July, and industry sources said it now may take until later this year before the hangover from an increased sales tax wears off.
Vehicle sales fell to 471,623 units in July, down 10.1 from a year earlier, the fourth straight decline on a year-on-year basis, the Japan Automobile Dealers' Association said on Friday.
"In view of the weak July sales, domestic sales may not recover until September when Japanese and foreign carmakers introduce new models," an association official told Reuters.

The sales tax increase to five percent from three percent on April 1 has taken the steam out of auto sales in Japan, with year-on-year declines of 12.7 percent in April, 9.4 percent in May and 5.0 percent in June.
Big automakers such as Toyota Motor Corp said they are hoping for a turnaround in September and a boost from the Tokyo Motor Show in late October.
"Maybe we will not see a recovery until September," a Toyota spokesman said. "We hope this year's motor show and new models from all the carmakers will stimulate demand."
Carmakers launch new models in late August ahead of the motor show, which is held once in every two years from late October until early November.

Toyota's sales fell 9.1 percent in July on a year-on-year basis, while Nissan Motor saw its sales fall 13.0 percent, Honda Motor 11.6 percent, Mitsubishi Motors 7.4 percent and Mazda Motor 0.6 percent.

The Toyota spokesman said one factor supporting a rebound in sales was the large latent replacement demand from consumers who bought cars during "bubble economy" of inflated asset prices in the late 1980s.

Toyota executive vice president Kanji Kurioka said recently that there has been an increase in the number of visitors to Toyota's showrooms, but it had not translated into actual sales yet because of the bigger sales tax bite.
Honda Motor Co Ltd president Nobuhiko Kawamoto also said the market undertone was weak because of the sales tax.
The only Japanese carmakers to increase their sales in July were Suzuki Motor Corp and Daihatsu Motor Co Ltd, whose recreational vehicles were in good demand.
Analysts also said weak housing starts, slow department store sales and a growing racketeer scandal involving several Japanese brokerages and a bank were hurting sales.

"The increased sales tax is one main factor for the poor sales. Another factor is concern about employment. That's why housing starts remain weak and people aren't buying new cars," said Seiji Sugiura, a car industry analyst at Nomura Securities Co Ltd.
The government announced earlier on Friday that the seasonally adjusted unemployment rate in June stood at a record high of 3.5 percent for the second successive month.
Sugiura said he was pessimistic about any rebound in domestic sales for the rest of the year.

He said because sales jumped before the tax increase, he was expecting a fall of 11 percent in July-September period this year over the same period in 1996, a 6.3 percent fall in the October-December period and a 9.8 percent drop in the January-March period.
Sugiura predicted that domestic sales for all of 1997 would fall by about three percent from a year earlier to 5.21 million units.
